METODOLOGÍA DE TRABAJO CON CLAUDE CODE (RESUMEN)
================================================

Proyecto: análisis de un conjunto de 31 artículos científicos (PDF) sobre la
programación de hornos y de la producción de acero con criterios energéticos,
realizado en cinco tareas encadenadas.

Herramienta: Claude Code (aplicación de escritorio), como asistente que
ejecuta las acciones. Se usó Python (con las librerías matplotlib y networkx),
Poppler/pdftotext para extraer el texto de los PDF y pandoc para generar los Word.

PRINCIPIOS SEGUIDOS
-------------------
- Solo cuenta como evidencia lo que dicen los documentos del conjunto.
  No se inventan datos, autores, cifras ni relaciones.
- Se distingue siempre entre evidencia directa y [interpretación].
- Toda afirmación importante indica los documentos que la respaldan (D1–D31).
- Las citas literales y las cifras se comprobaron automáticamente contra el
  texto original de los PDF.
- Cada tarea se limitó a su propio alcance, sin adelantar trabajo de las
  siguientes.

TAREA 1 – INVENTARIO Y EXPLORACIÓN INICIAL
------------------------------------------
1. Recuento y tipo de todos los archivos: 31 PDF, todos legibles.
2. Extracción automática del texto con pdftotext (texto completo, primeras
   páginas y primera página por separado). Las páginas con texto ilegible se
   recuperaron con otros modos de extracción (modo "raw" y codificación UTF-8).
3. Extracción de los metadatos de cada documento (título, autores, revista,
   fecha y palabras clave) a partir de su propio texto. Los campos ausentes se
   marcaron como "Not found".
4. Extracción de un fragmento literal breve de cada documento, con la
   interpretación separada del texto citado.
5. Matriz de frecuencia de términos (Python) para detectar los temas y
   comprobar si ciertos temas estaban ausentes.
6. Redacción del informe: inventario, fragmentos, temas, límites del dominio,
   fuentes de complejidad, herramientas y control de calidad.

TAREA 2 – MAPA TOPOGRÁFICO
--------------------------
1. Asignación de cada documento a conceptos concretos, según su título,
   resumen, palabras clave y caso de estudio.
2. Árbol jerárquico de temas: dominio → 5 temas principales → 21 subtemas →
   62 conceptos, con los documentos que respaldan cada uno.
3. Detección automática de las citas entre documentos del propio conjunto,
   buscando cada título en las bibliografías (se encontraron 4 citas).
4. Red de referencias cruzadas (networkx). Cada conexión indica su base:
   cita, autores compartidos, mismo problema, mismo método o perspectiva
   (esta última marcada como interpretación).
5. Métricas de red: grado, centralidad de intermediación, puentes y
   detección de comunidades, más una matriz de coincidencia entre subtemas.
6. Diagramas con matplotlib, revisados visualmente y corregidos hasta que
   fueron legibles.
7. Análisis de dónde se concentra el conocimiento, qué zonas quedan aisladas,
   y control de calidad.

TAREA 3 – DIVERGENCIA DE ENFOQUES
---------------------------------
1. Selección de 6 subtemas a partir de la Tarea 2: los más cubiertos por los
   documentos o los que menciona el enunciado (DRL, gemelo digital, XAI y
   restricciones metalúrgicas).
2. Tablas comparativas de enfoques con sus ventajas, limitaciones,
   requisitos y compromisos, según lo que declara cada documento.
3. Mapa visual de la divergencia y tabla de compromisos transversales,
   sin combinar todavía los enfoques.

TAREA 4 – SÍNTESIS INTEGRADORA
------------------------------
1. Principios de diseño derivados de las Tareas 1 a 3.
2. Blueprint conceptual en cuatro capas (datos → gemelo digital y modelo de
   restricciones → DRL, optimización y XAI → decisión humana y ejecución),
   con dos bucles de retroalimentación.
3. Para cada componente se explica su papel y la solidez de la evidencia que
   lo respalda. Se señalan las lagunas: ningún documento aplica XAI al acero,
   y no está resuelto cómo garantizar que el DRL respete las restricciones.

TAREA 5 – INFORME FINAL (AIDA)
------------------------------
1. Informe ejecutivo con la estructura Atención, Interés, Deseo y Acción,
   que sintetiza las Tareas 1 a 4.
2. Valor esperado expresado solo de forma cualitativa, sin cifras de
   beneficio inventadas.
3. Hoja de ruta en 7 fases, cada una con su punto de decisión.

GENERACIÓN DE LOS ENTREGABLES
-----------------------------
- Informes redactados primero en Markdown y convertidos a Word (.docx)
  con pandoc, más un script de Python que ajusta el formato: estilos, tablas,
  página horizontal para el inventario y pie de página.
- Verificación de cada Word: XML válido, encabezados, tablas e imágenes.
  Los documentos no se pudieron abrir para revisarlos visualmente.

LIMITACIONES GENERALES
----------------------
- El análisis se basa únicamente en los 31 documentos, no en datos de planta.
- Las conexiones por contenido y la agrupación de temas son decisiones del
  análisis, tomadas con reglas explícitas.
- El blueprint es conceptual y no se ha probado.

Task 1: Inventory & Initial Scan
Document Set analysis for energy-efficient steelmaking and furnace scheduling
Assignment context. An industrial organisation wants to reduce operational complexity, improve energy efficiency and deploy intelligent automation in a high-stakes industrial setting: steelmaking and furnace scheduling.
Scope of this report. This report covers only Task 1. It (i) extracts metadata and initial snippets from every document in the Document Set, (ii) scans the knowledge domain, (iii) sets its boundaries, (iv) acknowledges the complexity of the problem and (v) lists the tools and approaches the documents bring to it. It does not build a topic hierarchy or a cross-reference network, and it does not design a solution. That work belongs to Tasks 2–5.
Conventions.
D1–D31 are document IDs. They follow the case-insensitive alphabetical order of the filenames.
Quoted italic text is copied word for word from the source document.
Text marked [Interpretation] is the analyst’s reading, not a claim made by the source.
“Not found” means the field could not be located in the document text.
0. Processing Log
1. Document Inventory
Date convention. The date column gives the publication year printed in the citation line. Online or acceptance dates are added in brackets when the document prints them. A machine-readable copy of this table is in Task1_Inventory.csv.
Inventory profile.
Publication years span 2016 to 2026. The 2016 papers are D7 and D11; the 2026 papers are D9 (©), D10 and D16.
Publication types. 26 journal articles (D25 is labelled a “Perspective”) and 5 conference papers (D6, D11, D13, D15, D17). Nat Comput (D2) is counted as a journal.
Industrial setting. From each paper’s own statement of its application or case study, the documents fall into four groups (18 + 4 + 1 + 8 = 31):
Steel production processes (18): D2, D3, D5, D7, D9, D10, D11, D12, D14, D15, D17, D18, D19, D22, D23, D24, D26, D29. In this group, D11 (product reallocation), D14 (energy prediction) and D19 (rolling-parameter optimisation) are not scheduling papers.
Other heat-intensive or metal processes (4): a steel-hardening furnace at an automotive plant (D1), cast-steel heat treatment at a casting manufacturer (D27), forging (D30), and generic parallel machines with furnace/steel examples (D28).
Energy-intensive heavy industry (1): D21 (steel powder manufacturing facility).
General manufacturing or cross-domain, with no steel case (8): D4, D6, D8, D13, D16, D20, D25, and D31 (an aluminium cold rolling mill).
2. Initial Snippets
Each snippet is a short word-for-word excerpt from page 1 (abstract or introduction) of its document. The snippets are deliberately brief; each document’s full abstract is on its first page.
3. Initial Knowledge-Domain Scan
Topics are grouped loosely for readability. This is not the Task 2 hierarchy. The documents listed for each topic are ones where the topic appears in the title, abstract, keywords or case study. Documents that only mention a topic in passing (for example in related work or references) are listed separately as passing mention.
3.1 Industrial process areas and scheduling problems
3.2 Energy and sustainability
[Interpretation] Energy is the single most widespread theme. It appears as a central objective in most of the steel and furnace documents and is absent as an objective in the XAI and human-centric papers (D4, D6, D8, D13, D16, D20, D25).
3.3 Uncertainty, dynamics and disruption
3.4 Multi-objective trade-offs
Energy vs. delivery performance (tardiness). D7, D22.
Energy vs. makespan or completion time. D15, D30.
Energy (cost) vs. production efficiency. D12, D21, D27.
Robustness vs. stability. D2.
Several rolling and plan constraints plus power consumption per ton. D26.
Penalty costs vs. total start times (reheating energy). D29.
Integrated reheating and rolling objectives. D17.
Multi-objective counterfactual explanation generation. D8.
3.5 AI-related and digital concepts (verified presence)
4. Knowledge-Domain Boundaries
4.1 Clearly inside the domain
Scheduling of energy-intensive steel production stages, especially furnaces. The documents cover reheating furnaces (D10, D14, D15, D17, D23), hot rolling and hot strip mills (D2, D17, D26, D29), SCC and ladles (D3, D12, D18), steel heat treatment (D7, D22) and EAF-based steel plants (D9). Justification: these form the largest, most consistent cluster, and they match the assignment’s “steelmaking/furnace scheduling” focus directly.
Energy efficiency as a scheduling objective and constraint. Supported by 17 documents (§3.2).
Uncertainty and dynamic or robust scheduling. Supported by D2, D3, D5, D7, D9, D18, D23, D24 and D29 (§3.3).
Optimisation methods for these problems. Exact, metaheuristic and learning-based methods (§6).
Intelligent automation for scheduling decisions. DRL in steel and energy settings (D5, D9, D21) and digital twins in steel (D10, D19, D26).
4.2 Related but peripheral (supported by the documents)
4.3 Outside the domain (as evidenced by the Document Set)
Detailed metallurgy, product chemistry and furnace thermal design. No document takes these as its subject. They appear only as inputs (for example billet heating specifications in D15, the bilinear furnace model in D1). [Interpretation] They are treated as given process constraints, not as research topics.
Application domains named only as examples. Healthcare, finance, aviation, waste management and autonomous driving appear only as examples or references (D6, D8, D25). They are outside the domain.
Predictive maintenance, cybersecurity and carbon pricing / emissions trading. A term search found no occurrences of “predictive maintenance”, “cybersecurity”/“cyber-attack”, or “carbon price/tax/trading” in any document. These are not identified in the documents, even though they could seem relevant to steel.
Blockchain, federated learning, graph neural networks, quantum methods. These appear at most in a few passing mentions (1–2 occurrences in D2, D4, D10, D16, D20, D21, D29), never as a topic. They are not identified as domain topics.
5. Sources of Complexity
Each row gives the direct evidence (paraphrased unless quoted) and the supporting documents.
Differing perspectives in the documents (kept separate).
How to model uncertainty. D7 argues that fuzzy logic is computationally simpler than stochastic approaches. D3 uses chance-constrained programming with Monte Carlo simulation. D29 uses robust optimisation. D5 argues that stochastic optimisation needs precise distributions and that robust optimisation is conservative, and proposes DRL instead.
Role of AI vs. humans. D25 argues that AI should collaborate with humans (intelligence augmentation) rather than replace them. D16 makes a similar human-centric (I5.0) argument. D9, D21 and D31 aim at automated decision policies. [Interpretation] This is a genuine tension relevant to “intelligent automation in a high-stakes environment”.
Reported energy shares are not directly comparable. The documents measure against different bases:
Iron and steel’s share of energy use: “no less than 18%” of total industrial energy consumption (D12); “approximately 5%” of global energy consumption (D14); “8% of global energy demand” (D9).
Reheating’s share: “15–20%” of total steel-production energy and “60–70%” of rolling energy (D14); “over about 10 percent” of total steel manufacturing energy (D23); hot rolling “more than 10%” of the entire process (D17); heating of ingots before hot rolling “up to 70%” of process energy (D7).
These figures should not be merged into one number.
6. Tools / Approaches Being Brought to the Problem
The table lists what the documents actually use. It is an inventory, not a solution design.
Verification of named technologies.
DRL: present. It is central in D5, D9, D13, D20, D21 and D31. Only D5 and D9 apply it to steel plants; D21 applies it to steel powder manufacturing.
Digital Twins: present. They are central in D10, D16, D19, D26 and D31. D10 and D26 apply them to steel scheduling, and D19 to steel rolling-parameter optimisation.
XAI: present. It is central in D4, D6, D8 and D13, and D19 uses SHAP. No document applies XAI to steel or furnace scheduling specifically.
LLMs: present only in D20, a generic job-shop setting.
[Interpretation] The toolset therefore splits into two groups:
a mature optimisation toolkit that has been applied repeatedly to steel and furnace scheduling;
a newer set of intelligent-automation tools (DRL, DT, XAI, human-in-the-loop) that the documents apply to steel only partially.
Checking how well these two groups connect is work for later tasks.
7. Initial Findings / Conclusion
All 31 PDFs were read and inventoried. Metadata is complete for all 31 documents except where marked “Not found” or flagged (D15 keywords; D13 DOI and exact date; D9 volume).
Core of the domain. The Document Set centres on energy-aware scheduling of heat-intensive steel production stages, with reheating furnaces, hot rolling, SCC and heat treatment as the recurring stages. Uncertainty and multiple objectives run across most of these documents.
Where the complexity comes from. The documents consistently describe complexity arising from:
combinatorial hardness;
coupling between stages;
time-dependent thermal behaviour;
uncertainty;
conflicting energy and delivery objectives;
real-time requirements;
human trust and safety concerns.
Tools brought to the problem. They range from exact optimisation and metaheuristics to prediction models, DRL, digital twins and XAI. Human-in-the-loop and safety perspectives add a governance dimension.
What later tasks should focus on. Energy-efficient furnace and steel scheduling under uncertainty, and the intelligent-automation tools (DRL, DT, XAI, human-centric control) that could support it. Non-steel XAI, human-centric and generic DRL papers should be treated as supporting, transferable knowledge rather than as steel evidence.
8. Quality Control
Remaining limitations and uncertainties.
Unreadable or partial fields. D15 has no keyword list. D13’s DOI is font-encoded and unreadable, and its date is inferred only from the conference name “CPSL 2022”. D9 is an article-in-press with no volume or pages. D11’s symposium name is partly garbled; the recovered parts are “17th IFAC Symposium”, “Vienna, Austria” and “Aug 31 – Sept 2, 2016”.
Date conventions differ across publishers. Some documents print only a year. Where the citation year and the online date differ (for example D2: online 2017, issue 2019), both are given.
Term counts are only a screening aid. They come from automated text search and can include hits in reference lists. Every topic assignment in §3–§6 was confirmed from the abstract, keywords or case-study text, not from counts alone.
Absence checks are limited to exact search terms. “Not identified” statements (predictive maintenance, cybersecurity, carbon pricing) mean no occurrence of those terms was found. A concept described in different words could have been missed.
Setting classification is partly interpretive. Classifying each paper as steel or non-steel relies on the paper’s own description of its case study (§1). Borderline cases are D1 (a steel-hardening furnace at an automotive plant), D21 (steel powder manufacturing) and D28 (generic, with steel cited as an application).
Snippets are short by design. Each is a few words from page 1. The full abstracts should be read from the PDFs for Task 2.
No page images were checked. Figures, tables and scanned-only content could not be inspected; all 31 files did contain a text layer.

Topic extraction.
Each document was assigned to specific concepts using its title, abstract, keywords and case-study description, as extracted and checked in Task 1.
Further text searches were run on the original PDFs in this task. They confirmed, for example, deterioration effects in D2 and D23, parallel machines in D10, D27 and D28, and by-product gases in D7 and D24.
A concept was recorded for a document only if the document treats it in its own contribution. Mentions that occur only in related-work sections or reference lists were excluded.
Hierarchy.
Concepts were grouped bottom-up into 21 subtopics under 5 main topics, which together make up one domain root.
Every document appears in at least one branch. A document can appear in several branches, because each branch describes a different facet (process, objective, method, digital technology, human dimension).
Document network.
Nodes are the 31 documents. A link was created only when at least one of the five bases in the table below applies. Being in the same broad field was not enough.

Topic network. Two subtopics are linked when both are supported by the same documents. The strength of the link is the number of documents they share (Figure 4).
Thematic groups.

As a check, an automatic community-detection algorithm (greedy modularity) was run on the network. Its result is compared with the six groups in §7.
Metrics. For each document the following were computed with NetworkX:
degree: the number of documents it is linked to;
betweenness centrality: how often it lies on the shortest path between other documents;
bridges and articulation points: links or documents whose removal would disconnect part of the network;
breadth: the number of subtopics the document covers.

4. Explanation of the Topic Hierarchy
Five facets, one domain. The documents describe their work along five recurring facets:
where the problem sits (P);
what is optimised and what makes it hard (O);
how it is solved (M);
what digital infrastructure supports it (G);
how humans relate to the automated decision (H).
Coverage by facet. Every document has a process context (P covers 31/31). Most also state explicit objectives or problem traits (O: 27) and a solution method (M: 26). Only 8 documents each contribute to G and to H.
Processes follow the steel route. P1 → P2 → P3 mirrors the production sequence the documents themselves describe: ironmaking/steelmaking, then casting, then reheating and hot rolling, then cold rolling (for example D23’s introduction and D10’s abstract). P4 collects furnace processes outside that main route. P5 holds plant-wide energy networks rather than production stages. P6 holds documents with no steel or furnace case.
Objectives are layered.
O1 (energy) and O2 (production) are goals the documents optimise.
O3 (uncertainty) and O4 (structure) are traits the documents give as the reasons their problems are hard. This matches the complexity sources identified in Task 1.
Methods run from classical to learning-based. M1 and M2 are optimisation families. M3 and M4 learn from data or from interaction with the process. M5 evaluates or represents behaviour.
[Interpretation] The M1/M2 versus M3/M4 split is an organising choice. Several documents combine the two: D3 uses forecasting with a GA, D2 an SVR surrogate with NSGA-II, D5 DRL with ALADIN, and D9 DRL compared against MILP.
The G and H branches are narrow. Each rests on 8 documents, and several of their specific concepts rest on a single document (LLMs: D20; process safety: D25; Industry 5.0: D16).

Task 3: Synthesis Divergence
Divergent approaches to key subtopics of energy-aware steel and furnace scheduling
1. Purpose and Selection
Purpose. For a set of key subtopics from Task 2, this report sets out the different approaches the Document Set takes and compares them. It does not combine the approaches; that is Task 4.
How the subtopics were chosen. Six subtopics were selected from the Task 2 tree. Each one either:
is among the most widely covered (Task 2, Fig. 5), or
is named in the assignment brief (DRL, DT, XAI, metallurgical constraints).
Evidence rules.
Strengths and limitations are those stated or reported in the documents (D-IDs as in Tasks 1–2).
Numerical results are quoted only as reported by that document, for its own case. They are not comparable across documents.
[Interp.] marks the analyst’s interpretation.
2. Comparison by Subtopic
S1 Scheduling the energy-intensive operation
Key divergence. Exact methods trade speed for optimality. Metaheuristics and hybrids trade guarantees for scale. DRL shifts the computation to offline training so that online decisions are fast.
S2 Coping with uncertainty and disruptions
Key divergence. Approaches differ on when uncertainty is handled: before execution (robust, fuzzy), through prediction (forecasting), after an event (rescheduling), or continuously (learned policies). They also differ on how much they need to know about the uncertainty (full distributions for stochastic methods, bounds for robust ones, fuzzy numbers, or simulated experience for DRL).
S3 Representing the process (digital models and twins)
Key divergence. The approaches range from first-principles models to pure data-driven models, and from offline simulation to live, synchronised twins. [Interp.] In this set, only D9 (steel, electric arc furnace) and D31 (aluminium) describe a twin or systems model that is used to train or feed a DRL agent.
S4 Energy as an objective
Key divergence. Energy is treated as a quantity (consumption), a cost (prices), a state (idle energy) or a system balance (energy media). The multi-objective handling also differs: Pareto fronts (D2, D7, D17, D22, D26, D29) versus weighted sums (D30, D15).
S5 Encoding metallurgical and process constraints
Key divergence. Optimisation methods state constraints explicitly. DRL enforces them only indirectly (through the action space or rewards). [Interp.] This is the most significant gap for using DRL in a metallurgical setting.
S6 Trust, explanation and human role
Key divergence. One group of documents makes AI explainable (D4, D8, D13). Another makes humans an explicit part of the system (D16, D20, D25). The documents do not agree on how much autonomy AI should have: D25 argues for keeping humans involved, while D9, D21 and D31 aim at automated policies.
3. Cross-cutting Trade-offs
4. Summary of Divergence
No single approach in the set covers all six subtopics. Each document concentrates on one or two of them (consistent with Task 2).
The deepest divergences are:
explicit optimisation vs. learned policies (S1, S5);
the stage at which uncertainty is handled (S2);
automation vs. human-centred AI (S6).
Not established by the set:
a head-to-head comparison of DRL and optimisation on the same steel case (D9 alone compares DRL with MILP and PPO);
any XAI application to steel or furnace scheduling.
5. Limitations
Strengths and limitations are taken from each document’s own claims, which rest on different cases and metrics, so the reported numbers are not comparable across documents.

1. Purpose
This report re-converges the approaches compared in Task 3 into a single organisational and technical blueprint for intelligent, energy-aware furnace and steel scheduling.
It integrates the four elements named in the assignment:
Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)
Digital Twins (DT)
Explainable AI (XAI)
metallurgical constraints
Each is integrated only as far as the Document Set supports it.

2. Design Principles Derived from Tasks 1–3
3. Blueprint
The blueprint has four layers and two feedback loops. The subsections below answer the questions the assignment asks.
3.1 What information enters the system?
3.2 What role does the Digital Twin play?
Mirrors the process. It represents furnaces, slab logistics and heating / energy behaviour, and is kept up to date from plant data (D9, D10, D31).
Provides the training environment for DRL. The agent learns in the twin rather than on the real plant (D9: offline training on the systems model).
Evaluates candidate schedules by what-if simulation before release (D10 uses its twin inside the scheduling algorithm; D27 uses simulation-based evaluation).
Supplies forecasts of arrivals and energy (D3, D24).
The twin is paired with a constraint and knowledge model, so that simulation, optimisation and DRL all use one consistent set of limits. [Interp.]
3.3 What role do DRL and optimisation play?
DRL scheduling policy — proposes schedules quickly under uncertainty (prices, arrivals, disturbances), as in D5, D9 and D21. Multi-agent variants suit distributed units (D13, D21).
Optimisation and verification — checks every proposal against the constraint model. It also provides an MILP or metaheuristic benchmark and makes the energy-versus-delivery trade-offs visible (D9, D12, D22, D29).
Why both. Task 3 found that neither approach alone satisfies both online speed and explicit feasibility. The blueprint therefore keeps them complementary rather than choosing one. [Interp.]
3.4 How are metallurgical and operational constraints considered?
Encoded once in the constraint model:
holding-time limits and furnace capacity (D15);
no-wait flow and sequence-dependent furnace setups (D22);
deterioration of heating time with waiting (D2, D23);
rolling-unit and process specifications (D26).
Restrict the DRL action space, following D9’s domain-knowledge rules.
Checked as hard limits in the verification step before any recommendation is shown.
Simulated in the twin, e.g. how slab temperature and heating time change over time (D1, D10, D23).
Open issue. The documents do not show how to guarantee feasibility of a DRL policy under all metallurgical constraints (D9 names this as a gap). The verification step is the blueprint’s safeguard. [Interp.]
3.5 What role does XAI play?
XAI sits between the decision engine and the human, and answers three questions:
Why this schedule? Which inputs and constraints drove it (post-hoc feature attribution, e.g. SHAP as used in D19; interpretation diagrams as in D4).
What would change it? Counterfactual explanations at the system level (D8).
What does each alternative cost? Its energy and delivery impact, drawn from the optimisation layer.
Design requirements follow the trustworthy-AI criteria in D6 (human agency and oversight, transparency, accountability).
Evidence gap. No document applies XAI to steel or furnace scheduling (Task 2), so this element is transferred from generic scheduling work (D4, D8, D13).
3.6 How do recommendations reach decision makers?
Operator console. A planner or operator sees ranked recommendations, their explanations and key indicators (energy, tardiness, throughput). They accept, modify or reject each one, so human authority is retained (D25, D16).
Execution. An approved schedule goes through the MES and control systems to furnaces, mills and ladles, and to energy dispatch (D9 describes deployment through the MES).
3.7 How does feedback return?

5. Organisational Implications (high level)
Roles.

Executive Briefing: Intelligent, Energy-Aware Furnace Scheduling
Task 5 - Final Report and Strategic Storytelling (AIDA: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action)
Executive Summary
A — Attention: A Complex, High-Stakes Scheduling Problem
The stakes are high. The documents describe steel as heavily energy-dependent:
steel accounts for “8 % of global energy demand” (D9);
reheating furnaces use an estimated 15–20 % of the energy of steel production (D14);
heating before hot rolling accounts for up to 70 % of that process’s energy (D7).
These figures use different bases (see Task 1) and are cited only to show that the problem is significant.
Why the problem is hard (Task 1, §5):
Key message: the decision problem sits where physics, logistics, energy markets and people meet. No single conventional tool addresses all of them.
I — Interest: What the Analysis Revealed
1. Knowledge is rich but fragmented (Task 2).
Concentrated: energy objectives, structured scheduling problems and optimisation methods; reheating furnaces and hot rolling (the densest cluster).
Isolated:
XAI and human-centric work never connects to steel or energy work;
DRL and digital twins appear together only once (D31, aluminium);
only 4 citations link documents within the set.
2. Each approach has a distinct strength (Task 3):
Key message: the value lies in combining these strengths. The Document Set itself shows that this combination has not yet been made.
D — Desire: The Integrated Blueprint
How it works (Task 4):
Inputs: plant data, orders, energy context, metallurgical rules and operator knowledge.
Digital twin + constraint model: mirrors the furnaces and slab logistics, holds every metallurgical limit in one place, and provides what-if simulation.
Decision engine:
a DRL policy, trained offline in the twin, proposes schedules quickly;
optimisation verifies their feasibility and exposes energy-versus-delivery trade-offs;
XAI explains each recommendation.
Human authority: planners accept, modify or reject a recommendation; approved schedules are executed through the MES.
Feedback: execution data update the twin, and operator overrides improve the policy and the rules.
Expected value (qualitative, evidence-based):
What we do not claim: the Document Set provides no evidence of an overall energy or cost saving for the integrated system. The improvements reported by individual documents apply to their own cases and cannot be added together or transferred directly.
A — Action: Practical Next Steps
Governance and risks:
Human authority. Final decisions remain with planners (D25).
Risks named in the documents:
DRL constraint handling (D9);
reward design (D20);
data silos (D19);
trust in black-box models (D6, D13).
Mitigations: the verification layer, shadow mode, XAI and staged gates.
Decision requested: approve Phases 1–3 as a scoped pilot, with a review at each gate.
